## What a Multi100 analyst received {#inside-multi100-what-an-analyst-was-sent .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so I could see the original estimates
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, lifted from the abstract
- A pointer to the **data** – in our case, sixteen Eurobarometer waves you fetch yourself from GESIS
- No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things I was not told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness. Registered protocol: osf.io/7snkz
:::

::: notes
Multi100 handed a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of them. Let me show you what that was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was a published paper – the whole thing, not blinded, so I could see the original estimates, and if anything that pulls you towards the original answer. With it came the central claim of the paper in a single sentence, lifted from the abstract, and a pointer to where the data were held. In our case that meant sixteen Eurobarometer waves that I had to go and fetch from GESIS myself, under licence. What did not arrive was any instruction on method. Analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout: who the other analysts were, and what any of them were finding. The isolation was part of the design, because it is what makes the spread at the end mean something.
:::

## The paper in brief {#the-paper-for-now-in-one-slide}

::: {.small}
- Author: I will say **OA**, the original author, from here on
- **Does the EU economic crisis undermine support for the EU?** – 16 Eurobarometer waves, **2004–2013**, about **390,000** respondents in **27 countries**

::: {.claimcard}
"The results show, first, that *poor economic performances* **increase negative** and **decrease positive** *dimensions of EU framing*."
:::

- Macro predictors: **national unemployment** and **GDP growth**. Outcome: what people say the EU means to them, sorted into four framing scales
:::

::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic. The full methodological reading comes later in the course.
:::

::: notes
And here is the paper, briefly. We come back to it later and spend a long time inside it, so this is just enough to follow what happened. It is from 2016, in the European Sociological Review, and I will call its author OA, the original author, from here on. The question is whether the economic crisis undermined how people relate to the EU: sixteen Eurobarometer waves from 2004 to 2013, the crisis decade, about three hundred and ninety thousand respondents across twenty-seven member states. The claim we were handed is the sentence in the box. On the right-hand side sit two macro indicators, national unemployment and GDP growth; on the left, what people say the EU means to them personally, sorted into four framing scales. That is all you need for now, and when we return to the paper we take the whole thing apart.
:::

## The two Multi100 tasks {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit. Record one categorical conclusion: does the evidence support it?

::: {.fragment}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, four instructions arrived, quoted from my own Task 2 report:

> - produce a single, main result in terms of statistical families of z-, t-, F-, or $\chi^2$ tests (or their alternative or non-parametric versions).
> - disregard contextual variables related to the EU policies and party EU salience and party EU positions indexes in your analysis.
> - use the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** in your analysis.
> - use the **unemployment rate** as the measure for poor economic performance in your analysis.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether we agree. Task 2 makes our *numbers* comparable – you cannot average five answers to five different questions.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion on whether the evidence supports it or not. Once that was submitted, task two arrived with four instructions, and these are the words in which I received them, copied from my own report. Produce a single main result, as a z, t, F or chi-squared test. Disregard the contextual variables that concern EU policies and the salience of the EU and its position for the parties. Use the positive non-materialist form of EU framing, which is the cosmopolitan scale of the paper. And use the unemployment rate as the measure of poor economic performance. The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that second question can only be asked once everyone is answering the same question, which is what the instructions were for.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports their test statistic and its degrees of freedom, in whatever form their model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so a fixed-effects model fitted in Stata and a multilevel model fitted in R can be read on the same axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask: how far apart are five defensible answers?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the five are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the degrees of freedom behind each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, with its degrees of freedom – a t, a z, an F, a chi-squared. Those get converted onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised mean difference, so that somebody's fixed-effects model in Stata and somebody else's multilevel model in R can be placed on the same axis and read against each other. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread you are about to see is a spread among analyses that passed review. Putting five numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and much of the argument about estimands later is about what happens when they do not. The other is that the degrees of freedom fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence, and the next chart shows what happens when they do not.
:::


## The five analysts – Task 2 results {#our-five-one-sign-very-different-sizes .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: forest5
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# The five Multi100 analysts of the same claim (cases/eu-frames/data/reference_marks.csv, with
# the software and document format from cases/eu-frames/data/analysts5.csv), each placed on
# the degrees of freedom of its own inference; an open circle marks the value
# in the Multi100 record where it differs, which is PRL47 alone, converted on
# its respondent count. C6HJR highlighted. The label shows the software and
# the document format, because this chart also leads into the tools segment:
# the toolchain did not cause the spread, but every analyst shipped a
# runnable document, which is what made the spread diagnosable afterwards.
tools5 <- analysts5 |> dplyr::select(id = analyst_id, tool, document)
fa <- ref_marks |>
  dplyr::filter(id != "OA") |>
  dplyr::left_join(tools5, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    me      = id == "C6HJR",
    lab     = paste0(id, "   ", tool, "  ", document),
    differs = abs(r_recorded - r_placement) > 0.001
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(r_placement) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = lab))
fa_rec <- dplyr::filter(fa, differs)

ggplot2::ggplot(fa, ggplot2::aes(r_placement, lab)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded, xend = r_placement, yend = lab),
               colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded), shape = 21, size = 5.5,
             colour = grey_mid, fill = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded, label = sprintf("recorded %s", fmt_num(r_recorded))),
            vjust = -1.3, hjust = 1.05, size = 4, colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = me), size = 6) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = paste("r =", fmt_num(r_placement, 2))),
            hjust = 1.3, size = 4.5, colour = ncl_blue) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = ncl_blue, `TRUE` = orange)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.62, 0.06), labels = \(x) fmt_num(x, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "partial correlation r, on the degrees of freedom of each inference",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15)
```

::: {.small}
- All five estimates negative, with partial *r* from **`r fmt_num(min(five_r), 2)` to `r fmt_num(max(five_r), 2)`**, and one of the five not significant even by the errors of its own model
- Multi100 recorded PRL47 at *r* = `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "r_recorded"))` (open circle), because its *z* was converted on `r fmt_n(analysts5$n[analysts5$analyst_id == "PRL47"])` respondents
:::

::: {.src}
Task 2 results as recorded in the public Multi100 dataset (osf.io/q5h2c); PRL47 placed on the `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "df_placement"), 1)` Satterthwaite df of a course refit of its design (cases/eu-frames/data/reference_marks.csv).
:::

::: notes
And here are the five of us, on this one claim. All five found a negative effect, so on direction we were unanimous. On size, look at the spread: from minus point zero six, which is not significant even by the errors of its own model, out to minus point four five, more than seven times as large. The orange dot is me, at minus point two four. The open circle on the PRL47 row is the value that Multi100 recorded for that analysis, minus point zero zero six, because its z was converted on the number of respondents, as if every respondent were an independent test of a national unemployment rate. The filled dot puts the same statistic on the degrees of freedom of a refit of its design, and there it sits close to my own result. On the scale as recorded, the spread looked like two orders of magnitude, and most of that came from the conversion rather than from the analyses. Before we go anywhere near why the rest of the spread arises, look at the labels down the left-hand side, because there is a column there that I have not mentioned yet.
:::

## Software and document formats {#look-at-the-labels .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Two of us worked in **Stata**, three in **R**
- Within R, three different document formats: a plain `.R` script, an `.Rmd`, a `.qmd`
:::

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
The software did **not** cause the spread. There is no Stata answer and no R answer to this claim.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
But because each of us submitted a document that somebody else could **open and run**, it became possible, afterwards, to find out what *did* cause it.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
That is what the toolchain is for.
:::
::::

::: notes
Two of the five worked in Stata, three in R – and within R, three different document formats: a plain script, an R Markdown file, a Quarto file. Now, the tempting reading of that column is the wrong one, so let me rule it out straight away. The software did not cause the spread. There is no Stata answer and no R answer to this claim; every one of these models can be fitted in either. But the column does matter, and it is why the tooling is worth caring about. Because every one of us submitted a document that somebody else could open and run, it became possible afterwards to go and find out what actually did cause the spread. I have read the code of all four of the others, line by line, and later you will work through the same choices that they faced. That is only possible because of what is in that column. So – the tools.
:::
